newsitem.title: UK: Euro products outlook - Heat seen perkier on cold.
newsitem.headline: Euro products outlook - Heat seen perkier on cold.

text.p: European oil product prices could gain on strong heating oil demand this week provided the continent keeps shivering through a mid-winter freeze, traders said.
"It's going to be wild," one trader said. "End-users will be shocked by the prices they're going to see."

A bullish combination of frigid temperatures and low heating oil stocks held by consumers in Germany, the continent's largest heating oil market, could push prices for prompt material well above $230 a tonne, traders said.
Cargo premiums could move upwards towards Jan IPE +$10 from Jan IPE +5 seen at the end of last week, traders said. Barge premiums could build towards Jan IPE +$5, they added.

But traders say demand could be tempered by a build-up of stocks in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) region caused by ice blockages in European barge canals. The blockages have slowed deliveries from ARA to inland Germany and Switzerland.
Trade volumes and the rate of price increase could also be curbed by buyer resistance to the higher levels, traders add.
Low sulphur diesel is likely to remain quiet, with cargo premiums around Jan IPE +$9/10.
Gasoline markets are seen trading sideways but with U.S. buying providing small spikes higher between bouts of trade house profit taking.
Transatlantic trade is expected to remain the focus with demand across Europe seen staying thin.
Traders said that despite last week's U.S. stock builds and increased output by U.S. refiners, interest to move product transatlantic had not waned.
"The only problem is the expensive freight costs but anyone with pre-booked tonnage can still work the arb at a good profit," one trader said.

Spot naphtha markets may continued to mark time for a while but traders expect perceptions of fresh petrochemical demand for second half January to continue to support and even strengthen forward paper markets.
Fuel oil could enjoy a busier week as pent up demand filters into the market after the Christmas and New Year doldrums.
Low sulphur cracked fuel may experience more activity with the return of the main Med buyer into the market.
"It's cold and I think there is some pent up demand which could lead to a flurry of buying," said one trader.
If the demand is concentrated it could knock low sulphur prices up $1-2 a tonne, say some traders.
Others, however, claim there is plentiful supply with at least two northern cargoes of 50,000 tonnes apiece on offer in addition to several smaller-sized parcels.
End-user utility demand for high sulphur cracked fuel may also emerge given the recent cold snap gripping much of Europe which has led to increased electricity use.
